cues.text: Speaker 1: And you know, Holland, we are colorblind. We don't know what is yellow, what is black or what is white.
We we're always educated that all people are equal, so we could never imagine that anything like the Holocaust would happen in Holland.
Speaker 2: I heard about your story and we're here to listen a little bit more.

So today, what we're going to do, we're actually going to travel in a game map, and you will be able to explain us about what we're going to see and is it resemble that what you've been through, okay?
Speaker 1: Okay.
My name is Avraham Ruth. I was born in Holland in 1928.
I came from an Orthodox liberal family, we were together six children, two sisters and four boys. I must say that we had a very good life till the war became, till 1940.
Speaker 2: When was it when you felt like, okay, this is really happening, my life is on threat right now and I don't know how can I make it through?
Speaker 1: The first thing you feel, you are being put into a situation where you felt that you you are hunted, you're an hunted man.

The Germans started to persecute, first of all, the Jews. First, we couldn't go to school, then we couldn't go to shops, we couldn't go with the with the tramway, we couldn't go on bicycles, and you see here is written central station and so on.
You didn't travel with the tram. No, we had no transport, we had to go everything walking.
Speaker 2: Like walking.
Speaker 1: Yes.
One of the first days of the war with Germany, they bombed out Holland. It took us by complete surprise, which was never expected, that they would bomb out civilians.
Here you see a typical thing what they made is sandbags, because at that time people thought that the sandbags would save them from the Germans.

On the 15th of May in 1940, when the when the Germans declared their victory, I had a classmate of mine, a very good friend of mine, and his parents, so this family, the father, mother, and three children, they took their own life.
I was only at that time 12 years old. We knew that it's not going right, it's going wrong, and this was a constant feeling during the whole war.
The Jewish community started school for Jewish children.
I, myself, studied in a parallel class with Anne Frank.

But in this school it was very strange because you would go to school, you would never know what teacher would be the next day, or what child would disappear, and you didn't know if they went into hiding, if they went were sent to concentration camp.
And and when I see a class picture today, I I see about more than half of them, which I know had never returned. Teachers who never came back. Nothing.
In the beginning of the war in '41, my grandfather had a big house opposite the ghetto. Because it was opposite the ghetto, the Germans never came to us. In '43, they forced us to go to a ghetto.

In that ghetto, they started to provoke Jews who lived in the ghetto, and there were some special group of Jews who did not accept it and started fights in the ghetto, and that gave a good reason for the Germans to make the first transport to Dachau, and most of them were killed almost immediately after they arrived in Dachau.

There was a big house of orphans. The Dutch police came, and they didn't let anybody come near. They brought in trucks, and 170 children were sent all together in trucks to to straight to Auschwitz, and also none of them came back.
At a certain night in September, in on the Jewish New Year, came the Germans and they took at night my grandfather and two sisters. All of them were killed in Auschwitz.

The strange thing is that we never never believed that we would be exterminated. Maybe we were naive or my parents were naive, the Jewish people were naive, they never understood the what was going to happen to them.
They came also to our home, but my mother told them that I had cholera or something like that, and the Germans were deadly afraid of sicknesses, so they just decided to leave us alone at that night.

My father had connections with the Dutch underground, and then the Dutch underground brought us to various addresses, each of my brothers on a separate address, where we were hidden during the war. I for myself went up to a farmer in a small village in the south of Holland, and in that place there was a Catholic priest and he told some farmers in the neighborhood, "You have to take a Jewish child and you must and you have to hide them." And for that reason, in the same place, there were about 200 Jewish children who were saved.
If you see here the burning windmill, when I was hidden with a farm in in the south of Holland, about the same time, about 13 farmers around the farm where I was, they were burned down.
Speaker 2: Do you remember moments when you were hearing hearing fightings on the streets?

Speaker 1: No, the only the only thing I remember very well, if if we talk about war action, that was the fight around the Battle of Arnhem. The Battle of Arnhem was one of the greatest battles in in the Second World War, because they believed that if you take if they could take the bridge of Arnhem, they they could invade Germany and it would be the end of the war.
Speaker 2: You saw the parachutes?
Speaker 1: Yeah, I mean they came in the where I lived, they came all around me.
Speaker 2: You remember?

Speaker 1: Yeah, I remember personally very well, and also I I remember very well how the American parachutists came down, and the Germans shot at them, and there were many of these parachutists were killed and they were not able to get the the bridge and they lost.

We never talked at home about the Holocaust. The reason is that all of us who survived the war, we have a trauma. We have a trauma of the war, and we didn't want our children who live in Israel in a free country...
Speaker 2: To relive it.
Speaker 1: And they didn't want them to become a part of our trauma.
So this is one of the things I regret most.
Speaker 2: What do you think about it? This is this is insane that it actually happened less than 100 years ago. Now everybody more aware, more aware about race or or religion, but back then...

Speaker 1: When you see this you see this picture, this beautiful picture, and then you see life goes on, the sun is shining, the water is flowing, the boat is in the water, you would never believe that in this kind of place could be any war.

The the reason that I come here and the reason that I tell the story is that we want the the people, the world also, to remember and not to forget, and not to forgive. And it's my task as long as I live, to tell the people what happened so it won't happen again.

Speaker 2: I feel very related, not only as a Jew, but my my grandfather actually came from Austria, ran away from the Nazis with all of his family here to Israel. He was lucky one. And I remember as a kid, I was looking for his passport, just to see the the, you know, the the stamp of the Nazis, just to see that this is real. Because when I was a kid, we we taught, we were born and raised to never forget. So we really need to deliver this message to the youngsters, to the teens who haven't experienced this kind of stories from their own family. So this is why we're trying to deliver this message and to bring in bring it up to the spotlight again, especially in those social media...
Speaker 1: platforms. And, you know what's funny?
Most of us are playing games such as Call of Duty, Battlefield, stuff like that.
And when they see the cities, all burning down, all down to ashes, and they don't understand that this is actually happened.
This is actually a real views that people actually saw in their daily basis for
five, six years.
They felt haunted.
This is our legacy,
and we should never ever forget.
And we need to deliver this message to the next generations to come.
